extracted.intended_audience: chemists, natural philosophers, and physicians (readers of the Philosophical Transactions)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and empirical criteria for arguing about the origin, identity, and properties of alcaline/fixed/volatile salts and for practical laboratory and medical procedures (e.g., making laudanum). Emphasizes sensory tests, decomposition/combustion experiments, reproducibility, and procedural detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensory and physiological detection as evidence of pre-existing salts
rubrics_metrics.description: If a vegetable (or other substance) truly contained alcalies (fixed salts) pre-existing, it should 'manifest to the taste or by its effects' that it contained such a salt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues he 'never yet found' any vegetable, animal or mineral that betrayed the presence of alcalies by taste or effects; many plants that yield volatile salts do show taste/effects, so absence of sensory signs is used as evidence against pre-existence. (Used as a primary empirical test.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence in animals consuming plants as an indicator of pre-existence
rubrics_metrics.description: If alcalies were present in plants in appreciable amounts, animals whose sole food they are would also abound with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes lack of traces of alcalies in blood, urine, bones, horns, etc., of animals that eat such plants; uses this negative evidence to argue alcalies do not pre-exist in plants in the observed quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition after burning green vs dry as a test for production-by-fire
rubrics_metrics.description: Most vegetables burnt while green and with a smothering fire yield neutral or acid (tartareous) salts rather than alcalisate; only some dry herbs/woods yield alcalies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The observed salt type depends on whether the plant is burnt green or dry and on the firing method; thus if alcalies result chiefly from particular firing conditions, this supports production-by-fire rather than pre-existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results of fermentation/putrefaction vs calcination to determine natural components
rubrics_metrics.description: Fermentation/putrefaction of plants yields oil, acid spirit, and volatile salt copiously, while entirely putrified material yields little or no alcaly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because natural decomposition produces volatile salts and oils (which clearly pre-exist), but not alcalies, the absence of alcalies after putrefaction supports the claim that alcalies are produced by the action of fire (calcination) rather than pre-existing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of calcination/distillation experiments to adjudicate hypotheses about alkali origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Three possible accounts for how fire produces alkali are considered; the preferred hypothesis is that alcalies result from the union of volatile salt with the oleaginous (sulphureous) principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author marshals experimental facts (e.g., tartar calcined becomes alcaly; nitre with sulphur becomes fiery alcali; nitre yields acid spirit on distillation while still containing volatile salt) as criteria to choose among hypotheses about mechanism of formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior on mixing acids and alcalies as diagnostic of their nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Acids and alcalies heat, contend, and 'mortify' each other when mixed; this contrariety indicates essential difference rather than similarity of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If alcalies were near to acids in nature, they would unite quietly; violent reaction on mixing is taken as evidence of distinct natures and as an argument against viewing alcalies as acid-derived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement of properties between alcalies and volatile salts as evidence of common components
rubrics_metrics.description: Alcalies and volatile salts agree in many properties (diuretic, de-obstruent, dissolution of sulphureous bodies, contrariety to acids) except specific differences like gravitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarity of effects and actions is used to argue that alcalies may arise from volatile salts uniting with oil/sulphurous principles; experiments resolving alcalies into oil + volatile salt support this reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformations depend on degree of heat and method — control for comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree and manner of heating (calcination), space of time, and added substances strongly affect the salts produced; thus differences observed between salts of different plants may reflect method not intrinsic difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author repeatedly emphasises that tartar and other substances produce different salts under gentle vs intense calcination; to compare salts one must standardize heating conditions, time, and procedure to avoid spurious differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separability of alcalies into oil and volatile salt by experimental methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Alcalies can be divided into an oil and a volatile salt by 'easy and natural methods'; the whole body of alcalies has been resolved into these two substances in experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful separation experiments (including independent confirmations) are presented as proof that alcalies are compound and not simple; separability is a methodological criterion for chemical composition claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purification/rectification removes vegetal-specific properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Salts 'perfectly alcalised' and highly rectified do not differ sensibly from each other; apparent medicinal differences often stem from retained essential oils or partial calcination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues that the medicinal 'specific' properties attributed to salts of particular plants are due to residual oils or partial processing; full purification reduces salts to a common standard — so degree of purification must be considered when claiming specific properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source material and processing conditions must be specified for reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Pot-ashes and other products vary with the wood or plant (green or dry), their oily/aqueous/acetous content, and the degrees of heat used; such variability explains inconsistent industrial outcomes (e.g., glassmaking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To achieve reproducible chemical/industrial results, practitioners must report and control source material (species, moisture), firing conditions, and additives; variability in these factors accounts for observed differences across batches or reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laudanum Helmontii Junioris preparation procedure (production guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed recipe: opium 1/4 pound; quince juice ~4–5 pounds; opium thinly sliced/minced, mixed with luke-warm liquor and fermented at moderate heat for 8–10 days; filter; infuse cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves (1 oz each) 3–7 days; boil a walm or two after spices; evaporate to extract consistency; incorporate 2 ounces powdered saffron; adjust evaporation for pills vs liquid; doses: liquid 5–10 drops, pills somewhat less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes small variations (use of 5 pounds juice, half-ounce more spice, straining through canvas bag, use of saffron extract) and recommends following the annexed paper's method; gives form-specific evaporation advice and dosing guidance according to consistency and circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morbid anatomy should be based on diseased corpses to inform practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The main utility for a physician/surgeon is to know the constitution of parts as they occur in remarkable diseases; anatomy useful in practice is composed from inspection and consideration of subjects dead of those diseases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author recommends examining situation, shape, colour, connection, substance, etc., of brain, lungs, liver, intestines, etc., in cases of apoplexy, epilepsy, consumption, fevers, dropsy, jaundice, small-pox, cough, etc., to better understand affected places and conjoint causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation criteria for a new surgical (lithotomy) method
rubrics_metrics.description: A surgical procedure should be assessed for: applicability across patient bodies (e.g., corpulent adults), operator's ability to reach the target (bladder), expected pain/torture caused, correctness/timing of procedural steps (e.g., positioning before introducing fingers), consistency in operative duration and outcomes, and presence of expected postoperative signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author critiques the new lithotomist on grounds including: method unlikely usable on very corpulent patients or large/adhesive stones; procedure likely torturing; suspicious insertion of fingers before posture; great variability in operation time (2–30 minutes) suggestive of deception; absence of expected postoperative urine flow and prolonged cicatrix formation; advocates verifying claims by sounding and autopsy (e.g., finding stone post-op or not) as objective tests.
